what_its_for: Abaloparatide is used to treat osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) in women who have gone through menopause and are at high risk for bone fractures (broken bones). It works by stimulating your body to build new bone, making your bones stronger and less likely to break.
how_to_take: Abaloparatide comes as a solution in a prefilled pen that you inject under your skin (subcutaneously). You will inject it into your belly (abdomen) area, at least 1 inch away from your belly button. Rotate injection sites each day to avoid injecting in the same spot. Sit or lie down when giving yourself the injection, and stay seated or lying down for a few minutes afterward to prevent dizziness. Your healthcare provider or pharmacist will show you exactly how to use the pen before you give yourself your first injection. Always use a new needle for each injection.
dosing: The usual dose is 80 micrograms (mcg) injected once daily under the skin. Always follow your doctor's instructions. Do not inject more than once per day. The total treatment period is usually no more than 2 years (24 months) over your lifetime.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, give it as soon as you remember on that same day. If you do not remember until the next day, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at your regular time. Never give yourself two doses in one day to make up for a missed dose.
storage: Store your new, unused pens in the refrigerator (36°F to 46°F or 2°C to 8°C). Do NOT freeze abaloparatide. Once you start using a pen, keep it at room temperature (68°F to 77°F or 20°C to 25°C) and use it within 30 days. Do not put an opened pen back in the refrigerator. Keep the pen cap on when you are not using it. Keep this medication out of the reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Avoid standing up too quickly right after your injection, as this can cause dizziness or fainting. Avoid injecting into areas that are red, bruised, tender, or have scars or stretch marks. Do not share your pen or needles with anyone else, even if the needle has been changed, as this can spread infection. Avoid lying in the sun for extended periods, as this medication can slightly increase calcium levels — your doctor will monitor this.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get medical help right away if you experience: fast or pounding heartbeat, dizziness, or lightheadedness (especially after injection); nausea or vomiting that is severe; leg cramps or muscle weakness; increased thirst or urination, or confusion (these may be signs of high calcium in your blood); pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site that does not go away; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, itching, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing; back pain or bone pain that is new or unusual; or any other symptoms that worry you.
when_it_works: Abaloparatide starts working to build bone right away, but it may take several months before you notice a difference in your bone strength. Most people see significant improvement in bone density after about 6 to 12 months of regular use. Your doctor will order bone density scans (DEXA scans) periodically to check how well the medication is working for you. It is very important to take it every day as prescribed.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): This medication is commonly used in this age group and is generally safe, but older adults may be more sensitive to dizziness after injection — take extra care when sitting or standing up. Kidney problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney disease, as dose adjustments or extra monitoring may be needed. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medication is only approved for use in postmenopausal women. It should NOT be used during pregnancy or while breastfeeding. Children and teenagers: This medication is not approved for use in children or adolescents whose bones are still growing. Bone cancer risk: This medication carries a boxed warning (the most serious type of FDA warning) about a potential increased risk of a rare type of bone cancer called osteosarcoma, based on animal studies. Talk to your doctor about your personal risks and benefits. Do not use this medication if you have Paget's disease of bone, unexplained high blood calcium (hypercalcemia), or if you have had radiation therapy to your bones.
